note: 50 questions, all one level. Built for surprise while staying guessable. Every citation points at a source retrieved during research.

questions.prompt: How many people live in slums or informal settlements without basic services?
questions.whyCorrect: 1.12 billion — roughly one in seven people alive. No secure water, sanitation, or legal right to stay where they live.
questions.action: Look up what services define an 'informal settlement'.

questions.prompt: What share of the world's population lives in cities?
questions.whyCorrect: Over half already — and heading for 70% by 2050. Humanity became an urban species in about 2007.
whyWrong: Cities passed the halfway mark years ago.
questions.action: Find out what year your country became majority urban.

questions.prompt: By 2050, what share of people will live in cities?
questions.whyCorrect: 70% — meaning nearly all future population growth happens in cities, most of it in Africa and Asia.
whyWrong: Urban share is rising, not falling.
questions.action: Ask where the next billion city-dwellers will live.

questions.prompt: How much of their income does the average household spend on housing?
questions.whyCorrect: 31.0% globally — nearly a third of everything earned, before food, transport or anything else.
whyWrong: Too high for the global average.
questions.action: Work out 31% of a $2,000 monthly income.

questions.prompt: In sub-Saharan Africa, housing costs take what share of income?
questions.whyCorrect: 43.5% — the highest in the world. Nearly half of income goes on shelter, in the region with the lowest incomes.
questions.action: Ask what a family cuts when rent takes 43% of income.

questions.prompt: Housing costs in Europe and Northern America take what share of income?
questions.whyCorrect: 21.4% — the lowest measured share, and roughly half sub-Saharan Africa's 43.5%. Richer places spend proportionally less on shelter.
questions.action: Compare 21.4% with 43.5% and ask why the gap exists.

questions.prompt: How many people worldwide struggle to afford housing?
questions.whyCorrect: Between 1.6 and 3 billion — up to a third of humanity cannot afford adequate housing. It is a global crisis, not a local one.
questions.action: Ask what makes housing unaffordable where you live.

questions.prompt: How much green space did the average city have in 1990 versus 2020?
questions.whyCorrect: Fell from 19.5% to 13.9% — cities lost more than a quarter of their green space in thirty years, exactly when they needed it most for cooling.
whyWrong: The trend is the opposite — green space shrank.
questions.action: Find the nearest park and time how long it takes to walk there.

questions.prompt: How many urban residents could face at least 0.5°C extra warming by 2040?
questions.whyCorrect: 2 billion. Cities heat up faster than the countryside because concrete and asphalt store heat — the 'urban heat island' effect.
questions.action: Compare a shaded street with a bare one on a hot day.

questions.prompt: What share of city-dwellers may face annual average temperatures of 29°C or higher?
questions.whyCorrect: 36% — over a third of urban humanity living in year-round heat that makes outdoor work dangerous.
questions.action: Look up the average annual temperature where you live.

questions.prompt: How many people live in areas at risk of severe river flooding?
questions.whyCorrect: 1 billion people, as of 2025. Cities grew along rivers for water and trade — and that is exactly where floods arrive.
questions.action: Find the nearest river to your home and its flood history.

questions.prompt: Since 1975, urban flood exposure compared with rural has grown to:
questions.whyCorrect: 3.5 times rural exposure. Cities expanded into floodplains faster than anywhere else, putting more people in harm's way.
whyWrong: Urban exposure grew far faster than rural.
questions.action: Ask why building on a floodplain is tempting.

questions.prompt: How much do cities need each year for climate action through 2030?
questions.whyCorrect: $4.5–5.4 trillion a year. Cities currently receive $831 billion — roughly a sixth of what's needed.
questions.action: Compare $831 billion with $5 trillion.

questions.prompt: Cities received $831 billion a year in climate finance. What share went to adaptation — preparing for impacts?
questions.whyCorrect: Just over 1%. Almost all climate money goes to cutting emissions; almost none goes to protecting people from heat and floods already arriving.
questions.action: Ask what the difference is between mitigation and adaptation.

questions.prompt: How many pieces of infrastructure are damaged or destroyed by disasters each year?
questions.whyCorrect: About 92,199 units a year — schools, clinics, roads, power lines — causing over 1.6 million service disruptions annually.
questions.action: Ask what happens to a town when its clinic floods.

questions.prompt: How many service disruptions do disasters cause annually?
questions.whyCorrect: Over 1.6 million every year — each one a hospital without power, a school closed, or a water supply cut.
questions.action: Ask what your school does when the power fails.

questions.prompt: What share of cities have strong civil society participation in urban planning?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 19%. In most cities, decisions about where people live and travel are made without meaningfully consulting the people affected.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic — most cities score low.
questions.action: Find out how your town consults residents on planning.

questions.prompt: What share of cities have very limited or NO public participation in planning?
questions.whyCorrect: 29% — nearly a third of cities plan with essentially no public input, and another 35% have only low participation.
questions.action: Ask who decides where a new road goes in your area.

questions.prompt: Which region collects the least municipal waste?
questions.whyCorrect: Sub-Saharan Africa at 62.6% — over a third of waste is never collected, so it burns, blocks drains or pollutes water.
questions.action: Ask where uncollected rubbish actually ends up.

questions.prompt: Waste collection in Europe and Northern America reaches:
questions.whyCorrect: 99.4% — essentially universal, and so routine that most residents never think about it. In sub-Saharan Africa it is 62.6%.
whyWrong: Coverage is far higher than this.
questions.action: Find out where your household waste goes after collection.

questions.prompt: Eastern and South-Eastern Asia collect what share of municipal waste?
questions.whyCorrect: 64.7% — surprisingly low for a region with many wealthy cities, because coverage varies enormously between and within countries.
whyWrong: That's closer to Northern Africa and Western Asia.
Too pessimistic — about two-thirds is collected.
questions.action: Ask why waste collection lags behind economic growth.

questions.prompt: How many countries have a national urban policy?
questions.whyCorrect: 68 countries as of 2023 — barely a third of the world, even though 70% of people will live in cities by 2050.
whyWrong: Far too high — most countries have none.
More countries than this have one.
questions.action: Find out whether your country has an urban policy.

questions.prompt: Of countries with national urban policies, what share strengthen local government finances?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 49% — fewer than half. Cities are handed responsibilities without being handed the money to meet them.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic — under half address local funding.
questions.action: Ask where your local council's money comes from.

questions.prompt: How much does the world spend per person on protecting cultural heritage?
questions.whyCorrect: A global median of $21.22 a year — but $83.30 in developed countries against just $3.86 in developing ones.
questions.action: Name a heritage site near you and ask who maintains it.

questions.prompt: Developed countries spend $83.30 per person on heritage. Developing countries spend:
questions.whyCorrect: $3.86 — a 22-fold gap. The countries with the oldest heritage often have the least money to protect it.
whyWrong: Far above the actual developing-country spend.
questions.action: Look up a heritage site that has been lost or damaged.

questions.prompt: How many countries report local disaster risk reduction strategies?
questions.whyCorrect: 110 countries, with an average of 73% of their municipalities actually implementing them — real progress on preparedness.
whyWrong: More than there are UN member states with such plans.
questions.action: Find out if your town has a disaster plan.

questions.prompt: In countries with disaster strategies, what share of municipalities implement them?
questions.whyCorrect: 73% on average — a national plan on paper only helps if local councils act on it, and roughly a quarter still don't.
whyWrong: Implementation is far higher than this.
Implementation is strong but not universal.
questions.action: Ask what a school's fire drill has in common with a city's flood plan.

questions.prompt: 1.12 billion people in slums is roughly what share of humanity?
questions.whyCorrect: Roughly 1 in 7 people. Slums are not an edge case — they are how a seventh of the human race lives.
questions.action: Divide 8 billion by 1.12 billion.

questions.prompt: The 'urban heat island' effect means cities are:
options: Hotter, because concrete and asphalt absorb and hold heat
questions.whyCorrect: Hard dark surfaces absorb sunlight and release it slowly, so cities can be several degrees hotter — which is why losing green space matters so much.
whyWrong: The effect works the other way.
The temperature difference can be several degrees.
questions.action: Touch pavement and grass on the same sunny day.

questions.prompt: Green space in cities fell by roughly what proportion between 1990 and 2020?
questions.whyCorrect: From 19.5% down to 13.9% — a loss of more than a quarter of city greenery, mostly built over.
whyWrong: Green space shrank, it did not grow.
questions.action: Look at an old photo of your neighbourhood.

questions.prompt: Northern Africa and Western Asia collect what share of municipal waste?
questions.whyCorrect: 94.8% — close to European levels and far above sub-Saharan Africa's 62.6%. Waste systems don't track income perfectly.
whyWrong: That's closer to Eastern and South-Eastern Asia.
questions.action: Ask what makes a waste collection system work well.

questions.prompt: Latin America and the Caribbean collect what share of municipal waste?
questions.whyCorrect: 90.6% — strong coverage, well ahead of Eastern and South-Eastern Asia's 64.7% despite comparable income levels.
questions.action: Compare 90.6% with sub-Saharan Africa's 62.6%.

questions.prompt: What share of national urban policies address population change?
questions.whyCorrect: 87% — most urban policies do think about who is arriving and how many. The weak point is funding, at only 49%.
questions.action: Ask how your town's population changed in ten years.

questions.prompt: Cities get roughly what fraction of the climate finance they need?
questions.whyCorrect: $831 billion against a $4.5–5.4 trillion need — roughly one sixth. The gap is the single biggest obstacle to climate-ready cities.
questions.action: Divide $831 billion by $5 trillion.

questions.prompt: Why does living in a slum matter beyond the housing itself?
options: No secure tenure means no address, which blocks school, banking, healthcare and voting
questions.whyCorrect: Without a legal address, formal systems can't see you — so informal housing locks people out of services long after the roof is fixed.
whyWrong: Housing status shapes access to nearly everything.
Informal residents often pay high rents for poor housing.
questions.action: List five things you need an address for.

questions.prompt: Only 19% of cities have strong public participation in planning. Why does that matter?
options: Plans made without residents tend to serve investors over the people who live there
questions.whyCorrect: Who is in the room shapes what gets built — which is why participation is a measured SDG indicator, not just good manners.
whyWrong: Participation demonstrably changes what gets built.
Consultation can slow decisions but improves their durability.
questions.action: Find one planning decision near you and ask who was consulted.

questions.prompt: The number of countries tracking heritage spending tripled to:
questions.whyCorrect: 82 countries — tripled from previous reporting. Better measurement is itself progress: you can't protect what you don't count.
questions.action: Ask why counting something is the first step to funding it.

questions.prompt: 36% of city-dwellers may face 29°C annual average temperatures. That temperature is:
options: Dangerously hot as a year-round average
questions.whyCorrect: 29°C as an annual average means most days are far hotter — outdoor work becomes dangerous and cooling becomes a survival need, not a comfort.
whyWrong: That's a hot day, not a comfortable yearly average.
questions.action: Compare 29°C with your city's annual average.

questions.prompt: Sub-Saharan Africans spend 43.5% of income on housing and collect 62.6% of waste. Together this shows:
options: Cities there are growing faster than services and incomes can keep up
questions.whyCorrect: The region urbanising fastest has the least developed urban services — growth is outrunning the systems meant to support it.
whyWrong: Informal housing reflects lack of options, not preference.
questions.action: Look up the fastest-growing city in Africa.

questions.prompt: Adaptation gets just over 1% of urban climate finance. Adaptation means:
options: Preparing for impacts that are already coming — cooling, drainage, sea walls
questions.whyCorrect: Adaptation protects people from warming that is already locked in. Underfunding it means cities will face heat and floods unprepared.
whyWrong: That's mitigation, which gets nearly all the money.
questions.action: Name one adaptation your city could build this year.

questions.prompt: 1 billion people live in flood-prone areas. Most flood risk is worst for:
options: Informal settlements, often built on the land nobody else wanted
questions.whyCorrect: Informal settlements occupy the cheapest, most exposed land — riverbanks, steep slopes, floodplains — so disasters hit the poorest hardest.
whyWrong: Wealthier areas are typically on safer ground.
Urban flood exposure is 3.5 times rural.
questions.action: Find out which parts of your area flood first.

questions.prompt: Australia and New Zealand collect what share of municipal waste?
questions.whyCorrect: 98.9% — near-universal, second only to Europe and North America's 99.4%.
questions.action: Rank the six regions by waste collection rate.

questions.prompt: What share of national urban policies aim for balanced development across a country's territory?
questions.whyCorrect: 81% — most countries recognise that one giant capital city and neglected regions is a problem worth planning against.
questions.action: Ask what share of your country lives in its biggest city.

questions.prompt: Housing costs of 31% of income are considered:
options: Right at the edge of what's usually called affordable
questions.whyCorrect: 30% is the common affordability threshold — so the world's average household is already at the limit, and sub-Saharan Africa is far past it at 43.5%.
whyWrong: Nearly a third of income is a heavy burden.
It is manageable, though tight — 43.5% is the crisis level.
questions.action: Look up the 30% affordability rule.

questions.prompt: 35% of cities show 'low' participation and 29% show almost none. Combined, that means:
options: Most cities plan with weak or no public input
questions.whyCorrect: 64% of cities — nearly two-thirds — plan with little or no meaningful public involvement, against just 19% with strong participation.
questions.action: Add 35% and 29% and compare with 19%.

questions.prompt: Why is losing city green space especially dangerous now?
options: Trees and parks cool cities and absorb floodwater — exactly what warming cities need most
questions.whyCorrect: Green space fell from 19.5% to 13.9% just as 2 billion urban residents face extra heat. Cities removed their own cooling system.
whyWrong: Appearance is the least of it.
Green space measurably reduces temperature and flooding.
questions.action: Measure the temperature under a tree and in the open.

questions.prompt: Nearly 92,199 infrastructure units are damaged yearly. The biggest consequence is:
options: 1.6 million service disruptions — hospitals, schools and water supplies going dark
questions.whyCorrect: The damage cascades: one substation or bridge failing cuts services for thousands of people who were never in the disaster zone.
whyWrong: Repair cost is only part of the harm.
The disruptions are counted in the millions.
questions.action: Trace what stops working if your local power station fails.

questions.prompt: By 2050, 70% urban means most new city growth will happen in:
questions.whyCorrect: Africa and Asia hold nearly all future urban growth — which is why weak urban services in those regions matter so much for 2050.
whyWrong: These regions are already highly urbanised with slow growth.
questions.action: Look up the fastest-growing cities in the world today.

questions.prompt: The heritage spending gap of $83.30 versus $3.86 per person suggests:
options: Protecting culture competes with basic needs when budgets are tight
questions.whyCorrect: When a government must choose between a clinic and a monument, the monument waits — which is why international heritage funding exists.
whyWrong: The gap reflects budgets, not values.
Costs vary, but the 22-fold gap is about spending capacity.
questions.action: Find a World Heritage site that is listed as in danger.

questions.prompt: The single biggest Goal 11 challenge is:
options: 1.12 billion people in slums while cities grow toward 70% of humanity
questions.whyCorrect: Housing is where Goal 11 lives or dies: a seventh of humanity already lacks adequate shelter, and the urban population is still rising fast.
whyWrong: Green space has fallen by over a quarter.
questions.action: Find out how many homes your area built last year.
